## Statement

Let $A, B, C$ be sets.

Prove $A \setminus (B \setminus C) = (A \setminus B) \cup (A \cap C)$.

## Solution

let $x \in A \setminus (B \setminus C)$.
This means $x \in A$ and $x \notin (B \setminus C)$.
Because $x \notin B \setminus C$, we know $x \in B$ and $x \notin C$ is false.
The negation of "$x \in B$ and $x \notin C$" is "$x \notin B$ or $x \in C$".
We now have $x \in A$, and ($x \notin B$ or $x \in C$).
Using the distributive law for statements (Problem 13), (Recall $P \wedge (Q \vee R) \iff (P \wedge Q) \vee (P \wedge R)$) we then have $x \in A$ and $x \notin B$, or $x \in A$ and $x \in C$.
This means $x \in A \setminus B$ or $x \in A \cap C$, which proves $x \in (A \setminus B) \cup (A \cap C)$.
Repeat for all $x \in A \setminus (B \setminus C)$.
we have shown $A \setminus (B \setminus C) \subseteq (A \setminus B) \cup (A \cap C)$.

Now let $x \in (A \setminus B) \cup (A \cap C)$.
This means $x \in A \setminus B$ or $x \in A \cap C$.
Suppose first that $x \in A \setminus B$.
then we know $x \in A$ and $x \notin B$.
Because $x \notin B$, we know $x \in B$ and $x \notin C$ is false, so $x \notin B \setminus C$.
This shows $x \in A$ and $x \notin B \setminus C$, proving $x \in A \setminus (B \setminus C)$.
Suppose instead that $x \in A \cap C$.
Then $x \in A$ and $x \in C$.
Because $x \in C$, we know $x \in B$ and $x \notin C$ is false.
Hence we know $x \notin B \setminus C$.
Because $x \in A$ and $x \notin B \setminus C$, we have $x \in A \setminus (B \setminus C)$.
Repeat for all $x \in (A \setminus B) \cup (A \cap C)$.
we have shown $(A \setminus B) \cup (A \cap C) \subseteq A \setminus (B \setminus C)$. $\blacksquare$
